content: Chinese materia medica, commonly referred to as Chinese herbology, is a specialized field of study within traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). It encompasses the foundational theories of Chinese materia medica, as well as the study of crude medicinal substances, prepared herbal drugs, traditional Chinese patent medicines, and simple herbal preparations. This discipline investigates the sources, collection methods, preparation techniques, properties, therapeutic effects, and clinical applications of these substances. Chinese materia medica is deeply rooted in the theoretical framework of TCM and includes a wide range of medicinal substances, such as raw herbs, processed herbal pieces, and standardized herbal formulations. Chinese herbology is the art and science of combining medicinal herbs to create therapeutic remedies. It is one of the most significant modalities in TCM. Each herbal prescription is a carefully tailored combination of multiple herbs, designed to address the unique needs of an individual patient. Typically, a batch of herbs is decocted twice over the course of an hour to extract its medicinal properties. The formulation process begins with one or two primary ingredients that directly target the illness. Additional herbs are then incorporated to balance the formula according to the patient’s yin-yang constitution. Some ingredients are included to neutralize the toxicity or side effects of the primary herbs, while others act as catalysts to enhance the overall efficacy of the preparation. This intricate process requires extensive knowledge and experience, distinguishing skilled herbal practitioners from novices. Unlike Western medicine, which often focuses on the effects of individual active ingredients, Chinese herbology emphasizes the balance and interaction of all components within a formula. The holistic approach of TCM prioritizes treating each patient as a unique individual, tailoring remedies to their specific physiological and energetic imbalances. Chinese herbology utilizes a wide array of ingredients derived from various parts of plants, including leaves, stems, flowers, and roots. It also incorporates substances from animals and minerals. However, the use of parts from endangered species, such as seahorses, rhinoceros horns, and tiger bones, has sparked significant controversy. This has led to the emergence of a black market for poached animal products. In response, many herbal manufacturers have ceased using ingredients derived from endangered species. History of Chinese Herbology The use of Chinese herbs dates back thousands of years. The mythical figure Shennong is considered the first herbalist in Chinese tradition. He is said to have tasted hundreds of herbs, distinguishing between medicinal and toxic plants, and shared this knowledge with early agricultural communities. The earliest known Chinese pharmacological text, the Shennong Bencao Jing (Shennong Emperor’s Classic of Materia Medica), was compiled during the Han dynasty in the 1st century CE. It lists 365 medicinal substances, 252 of which are herbs. Earlier records, such as the manuscript Recipes for 52 Ailments found in the Ma Wang Dui tomb (sealed in 168 BCE), also document herbal prescriptions for specific conditions. Over time, subsequent generations expanded upon these foundational works. For example, the Yaoxing Lun (Treatise on the Nature of Medicinal Herbs), written during the Tang dynasty in the 7th century, provided further insights into herbal medicine. One of the most influential texts in Chinese herbology is the Compendium of Materia Medica (Bencao Gangmu), compiled by Li Shizhen during the Ming dynasty. This comprehensive work remains a cornerstone of Chinese herbal medicine and is still widely referenced today. Categorization of Chinese Herbs Chinese physicians developed several methods to classify herbs, including the Four Natures, the Five Tastes, and the Meridians. Early texts, such as the Ben Cao (Materia Medicae) from the Han through Tang dynasties, categorized herbs into three levels: Low level: Herbs with drastic effects and potential toxicity. Middle level: Herbs with medicinal and physiological effects. High level: Herbs that enhance health and spirit. During the Song-Jin-Yuan era (10th–12th centuries), the theoretical framework of acupuncture, rooted in Confucian Han philosophy, was formally applied to herbal categorization. This integration aligned herbal medicine with the Five Phases (Tastes) and the 12 Channels (Meridians). The Four Natures The Four Natures describe the degree of yin and yang in herbs, ranging from cold (extreme yin) to hot (extreme yang), with cool, neutral, and warm as intermediate states. The selection of herbs takes into account the patient’s internal yin-yang balance. For instance, herbs with a hot nature are used to treat conditions of internal cold or a cold constitution. Conversely, cold herbs are used to address heat-related imbalances. Sometimes, additional ingredients are included to moderate the extreme effects of a particular herb. The Five Tastes The Five Tastes—pungent, sweet, sour, bitter, and salty—each have distinct functions and characteristics: Pungent: Promotes sweating and invigorates qi and blood circulation. Sweet: Tonifies and harmonizes bodily systems; some sweet herbs also have a bland taste, which aids in draining dampness through diuresis. Sour: Astringent and consolidating in nature. Bitter: Dispels heat, purges the bowels, and dries dampness. Salty: Softens hard masses and facilitates bowel movements. The Meridians The Meridians refer to the specific organs or channels that an herb acts upon. For example, menthol is classified as pungent and cool, and it is associated with the lungs and liver. Since the lungs play a key role in protecting the body from external pathogens, menthol can help expel coldness from the lungs and eliminate heat toxins caused by external wind. Chinese Patent Medicine Chinese patent medicines are standardized herbal formulations that are pre-prepared for convenience. These medicines typically consist of dried and ground herbs mixed into a powder and formed into small, round pills, often bound with honey. While they are easy to use and suitable for long-term treatment of mild conditions, they lack the customization possible with individually tailored herbal prescriptions. The term patent in this context does not imply exclusive ownership of the formula but rather refers to the standardization of the ingredients and their proportions. All Chinese patent medicines with the same name will have identical formulations. The 50 Fundamental Herbs Chinese herbology identifies 50 fundamental herbs that are widely used in TCM. These include: Agastache rugosa (huòxiāng): Known for its aromatic and digestive properties. Astragalus membranaceus (huángqí): Used to strengthen the immune system and tonify qi. Cinnamomum cassia (ròu gùi): A warming herb that invigorates circulation and dispels cold. Ephedra sinica (má huáng): Commonly used to treat respiratory conditions and promote sweating. Glycyrrhiza uralensis (gāncǎo): A harmonizing herb that reduces toxicity and enhances the effects of other herbs. Schisandra chinensis (wǔ wèi zi): Known for its astringent and tonifying properties. These herbs, along with others on the list, form the foundation of Chinese herbal medicine and are used in various combinations to address a wide range of health conditions.
